prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: nearby rocks, shrubs, and the trail are roughly 0.5–4 m away, the hikers are approximately 3–8 m away, and the hillside and valley extend tens to hundreds of metres behind them. Across frames 1–5, the group shifts from right-of-centre to centre-left, back toward centre, and finally to the far-right edge, largely consistent with camera turning; in frames 2–3, one person enters the right foreground at about 0.5–1.5 m, within the camera wearer’s arm reach, and partly occludes the trail, vegetation, and other people. The nearby hikers stand about 0.5–2 m from one another, with some facing generally toward the camera and others sideways or away, although facing direction is clearer in RGB than in depth. Depth makes foreground–background separation and the foreground person’s closeness much clearer than RGB alone, but its brightness is not metric, distant terrain merges into broad bands, and sky/upper-boundary regions plus fine vegetation and person contours look unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only people: a small, partly cropped person appears at the right edge of frame 1; roughly three hikers cluster about 3–8 m ahead in frames 2–5; and a much larger foreground person occupies the right side of frames 2–3 at about 0.5–1.5 m. It clarifies which overlapping shapes belong to separate people and shows occlusion order—for example, the large foreground mask in frame 3 lies in front of the distant group—while the distant people are roughly 0.5–2 m apart and outside the camera wearer’s reach. Across the strip, the masks move right-to-left through frames 1–3 and then back toward the far-right boundary by frame 5; several masks become truncated at image edges, while RGB suggests mixed facing directions but the masks alone cannot reliably establish gaze or front-versus-back orientation. The map is unreliable for the broader scene because it omits the trail, rocks, plants, and terrain, misses or fragments parts of people, overlaps labels, and gives no direct distance scale or dependable arm/hand geometry.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects almost no distant bodies: it shows one small partial upper-limb configuration near the close right-side person in frame 3 and one larger but edge-cropped body skeleton at the extreme right of frame 5. These detections help expose joint arrangement and coarse orientation that are hard to separate in RGB, suggesting a bent arm in frame 3 and a partly visible upright person in frame 5, but they do not reliably show gaze direction or whether either person faces the camera wearer. The frame-3 joints belong to someone approximately 0.5–1.5 m away and plausibly within the camera wearer’s arm reach, whereas the frame-5 figure appears several metres away and partly outside the view; the other hikers remain about 3–8 m ahead and receive no usable skeletons. The map is highly incomplete: it misses most people, shows no magenta hands, cannot represent terrain or inter-person distances directly, and its sparse or truncated joints make turning, approach, retreat, occlusion, and reach estimates unreliable without the RGB and depth maps.
